<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- doesn't block -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>
try_it: Add defer to a script in a project and check it still works.

title: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are baked in at build
why_it_matters: Changing one in Vercel does nothing until you redeploy.
explanation: Next.js replaces NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables with their real values while building. The browser code contains the final text, not a lookup. So after changing one, trigger a new build. Server-only variables are read at runtime on the server.
try_it: Change a public variable, redeploy, and confirm the new value appears.

title: Quiz yourself on the code you shipped
why_it_matters: Understanding beats a working app you can't explain.
explanation: After each feature, ask the AI to write five questions about the code it gave you, then answer them without looking. Wrong answers show exactly what to study next. Over time, you'll need the AI less for basics.
try_it: Generate five questions about your last feature, answer them cold.

title: Stop the form from reloading the page
why_it_matters: Forms refresh the page by default, wiping your JavaScript state.
explanation: Submitting a form navigates by default. Call e.preventDefault() in the submit handler to stop that. Then read the values with FormData, using the name attribute of each input.
try_it: Make sure your input has a name attribute, or get() returns null.

title: Bottom nav that avoids the home bar
why_it_matters: Fixed bottom bars on modern phones collide with the gesture area.
explanation: Add viewport-fit=cover to your viewport meta tag, then pad fixed bottom elements with env(safe-area-inset-bottom). It is zero on devices without a notch or gesture bar, so it is safe everywhere. Great for PWAs and app-style layouts.
try_it: Add viewport-fit=cover to your meta tag and test a bottom bar on a modern phone.

title: Mistake: onClick={save()}
why_it_matters: The function runs during render, not on click.
explanation: Parentheses call a function immediately. onClick needs the function itself, not its result. Pass the name, or wrap a call in an arrow function when you need to pass arguments.
code:
<button onClick={save()}>Save</button>      {/* runs on render */}
<button onClick={save}>Save</button>        {/* runs on click */}
<button onClick={() => remove(id)}>Delete</button>
try_it: Search your code for onClick={ followed by a function name with parentheses.

title: Read query strings with searchParams
why_it_matters: Search pages and filters live in the URL, so they can be shared.
explanation: Server pages receive searchParams as a prop, holding the part after the question mark. Awaiting it is safe in all versions. Using the URL for state means refresh, back and share links all keep working.
try_it: Visit /?q=sql and read the output.

title: Read and build URLs with URLSearchParams
why_it_matters: Filters and pagination are easier to share when they live in the URL.
explanation: URLSearchParams parses the query string for you. get reads a value, set changes it, and toString builds the new text with proper escaping. It's much safer than slicing strings by hand.
try_it: Build a link with a search term that contains a space and an ampersand.

title: textContent vs innerHTML: a security gap
why_it_matters: innerHTML with user input lets attackers run code on your page.
explanation: innerHTML parses a string as HTML, so a comment containing markup can run scripts through event attributes. textContent treats everything as plain text. Use it by default, and only use innerHTML for content you fully control.
try_it: Search your code for innerHTML and check where each value comes from.

title: Upload a file to Storage
why_it_matters: File uploads power avatars, documents and your own client-side tools.
explanation: Pick a bucket with storage.from, then upload a path and a File object. Prefixing the path with the user's id keeps files organised and makes storage policies easy to write. Check error before assuming it worked.
try_it: Create a private bucket and upload one file from the dashboard first.

title: Why your absolute element flew away
why_it_matters: It explains every 'my badge is in the wrong corner' moment.
explanation: An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor. If none exists, it uses the whole page. Give the parent position: relative and the child's top and right values start making sense.
try_it: Remove position: relative from .card and see where the badge goes.

title: 'I don't know yet' is an okay answer
why_it_matters: How you handle gaps matters more than pretending.
explanation: If you're asked something you can't answer, say so, then show how you'd find out: check the docs, test a small example, read the error. Teams hire people who learn well. Bluffing is easy to spot and costs trust.
try_it: Practice finishing the sentence: 'I'm not sure, but here's how I'd find out...'

title: JSON: the text format of the web
why_it_matters: Every API and localStorage conversation uses it.
explanation: JSON is text that looks like a JavaScript object. JSON.stringify turns a value into text so you can send or store it. JSON.parse turns text back into a value. Functions and undefined don't survive the trip.
try_it: Stringify an object containing a function and see what disappears.

title: Measure before you optimize
why_it_matters: Guessing what's slow wastes time on the wrong things.
explanation: console.time and console.timeEnd give you a quick stopwatch around any code. For whole pages, use the DevTools Performance tab. Fix the thing the numbers point at, then measure again to confirm it really improved.
try_it: Time a function in your own project and write down the result.

title: Build locally before you push
why_it_matters: It catches errors that dev mode forgives.
explanation: npm run dev is forgiving. npm run build is what Vercel runs, and it fails on things like type errors and missing imports. Also, Linux servers treat Button.js and button.js as different files, even if your computer doesn't.
code:
npm run build
npm run start
try_it: Run a production build of your latest project and fix what appears.

title: Check that an npm package really exists
why_it_matters: Invented package names can lead you to install something malicious.
explanation: AI sometimes suggests packages that don't exist, and attackers sometimes publish fakes with those names. Before npm install, check the name on the registry, its publisher, and that others actually use it. This one command shows details.
code: npm view react name version
try_it: Check one dependency in your project: who publishes it?

title: Pass functions as props
why_it_matters: It's how a child component tells its parent something happened.
explanation: Props can be functions too. The parent passes a callback, and the child calls it with data when something happens, like a click. Name them onSomething so their purpose is obvious. Data flows down as props, events flow up through callbacks.
try_it: Add an onDelete prop to a list item and log which id was clicked.

title: Fix 'window is not defined'
why_it_matters: It is the most common Next.js error for people using browser APIs.
explanation: Server code has no window, document or localStorage, and components are first rendered on the server. Read browser values inside useEffect, which only runs in the browser. Store them in state so the page can update.
try_it: Move a localStorage read from the top of a component into useEffect.

title: Format money with Intl.NumberFormat
why_it_matters: Fintech-style screens need correct currency formatting.
explanation: Intl.NumberFormat formats numbers for a locale and currency, adding separators and symbols correctly. Keep amounts as integer cents in your data and divide by 100 only when formatting. Never build currency strings by hand.
try_it: Switch the locale and currency and compare outputs.

title: Private files need signed URLs
why_it_matters: Public links to private documents are a serious leak.
explanation: A public bucket serves files to anyone with the link. For sensitive files keep the bucket private and create a signed URL that expires. The second argument is how many seconds the link stays valid.
try_it: Generate a 60-second link and test that it stops working after.

title: Why your CSS is being ignored
why_it_matters: Specificity explains most 'my style does nothing' bugs.
explanation: When two rules clash, the more specific selector wins, not the later one. An id beats a class, which beats an element. Fix it with a better selector, not !important. Check DevTools: the crossed-out rule lost the fight.
try_it: Inspect an element in DevTools and find a crossed-out rule. Why did it lose?

title: Split your code with import and export
why_it_matters: One giant file becomes unreadable fast.
explanation: A module is a file that exports things and imports what it needs. Named exports are imported with curly braces and must match the name. A default export can be imported under any name. Modules keep your code organised.
try_it: Move one helper function from your main file into its own file.

title: Center anything with place-items
why_it_matters: Centering is a layout trick you will use every single day.
explanation: Grid can center a child both ways in one line. place-items is shorthand for align-items and justify-items. Give the container a height, otherwise there is no empty space to center inside.
try_it: Put this on a div with one heading inside, then resize the window.

title: Fixed widths break on phones
why_it_matters: A 500px box overflows a 360px screen and causes sideways scrolling.
explanation: A fixed width ignores the screen size. min() picks the smaller of two values, so the box shrinks on small screens and stops growing on big ones. margin-inline: auto centers it.
try_it: Open DevTools device mode at 360px wide and compare both versions.

title: Use gap instead of margins
why_it_matters: It removes the 'extra space on the last item' bug.
explanation: Flex and grid both support gap, which adds space only between items. No margin-right on every child, no special case for the last one. Add flex-wrap and the row wraps neatly on narrow phones.
try_it: Replace margins on a row of buttons with gap and delete the old margin rules.

title: map() builds a new array
why_it_matters: It is the tool for turning a list of data into a list of UI items.
explanation: map runs your function on every item and collects the results into a new array. The original array is not changed. Use it when you want the same number of items, each one transformed.
try_it: Predict what prices.map(p => p * 2) returns, then run it in the console.

title: Common mistake: forgetting await
why_it_matters: This one bug causes most 'why is it undefined' moments with fetch.
explanation: fetch returns a Promise, which is a placeholder for a future value. Without await you get the placeholder, not the data. Both fetch and res.json() need await inside an async function.
try_it: Remove one await and log the result to see the Promise object instead.

title: Myth: const makes things frozen
why_it_matters: Knowing this stops confusing errors with objects and arrays.
explanation: Myth: const values can never change. Fact: const stops you reassigning the variable, but an object's contents can still change. You can edit properties or push to an array, just not point the name somewhere else.
try_it: Declare a const array, push an item into it, then try reassigning it.

title: setState is not instant
why_it_matters: It explains why your console.log shows the old value.
explanation: A state update is scheduled, not applied on the spot. Inside the same function call your variable still holds the old value. The new value appears on the next render, so read it there.
try_it: Click the button once and compare the console value with what the screen shows.

title: Use ids as list keys, not index
why_it_matters: Wrong keys cause odd bugs when a list is reordered or filtered.
explanation: React uses keys to tell which list item is which. Index keys shift when items are added, removed or sorted, so inputs can keep the wrong text. A stable id from your data is safer.
try_it: Check your last list: is the key a real id, or the array index?

title: Clean up effects or leak timers
why_it_matters: Forgotten cleanup makes timers pile up and slows your app.
explanation: An effect can return a function that React runs before the next effect and when the component leaves the screen. Use it to stop timers and remove listeners, otherwise they keep running forever.
try_it: Remove the return line, hide the component, and watch the console keep ticking.

title: Only NEXT_PUBLIC_ reaches the browser
why_it_matters: A secret behind the wrong prefix is visible to every visitor.
explanation: Next.js sends only variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ to the browser. Everything else stays on the server. Never put a secret key behind that prefix, because anyone can read it in your shipped JavaScript.
code:
# .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_NAME=DevTok
DB_PASSWORD=server-only-value
try_it: Log both variables in a client component and see which one is undefined.

title: Your first API route handler
why_it_matters: Route handlers are how your frontend talks to your own server code.
explanation: In the App Router, a file named route.js inside a folder becomes an endpoint. Export a function named after the HTTP method, like GET or POST. Return a Response and Next.js sends it to the caller.
try_it: Create this file, run the dev server, and open /api/ping in your browser.

title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY in one query
why_it_matters: These three words cover most of the reads you will ever write.
explanation: SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE keeps only matching rows, and ORDER BY sorts what is left. Read it top to bottom like a sentence and you can write most basic queries.
code:
select name, price
from products
where price < 5000
order by price;
try_it: Write the same query for a table of your own with a different WHERE.

title: JOIN joins rows by matching ids
why_it_matters: Real data lives in several tables, and JOIN is how you combine them.
explanation: Orders store a customer_id instead of the customer's name. A JOIN matches that id to the customers table so you can show both together. The ON line says which columns must be equal.
code:
select orders.id, customers.name
from orders
join customers
  on customers.id = orders.customer_id;
try_it: Draw two small tables on paper and match the ids by hand first.

title: Row level security in two statements
why_it_matters: Without it, anyone with your public key may read your table.
explanation: Row level security makes the database check a rule for every row. First you turn it on for the table. Then a policy says who may do what. This policy lets a signed-in user read only their own notes.
try_it: Turn RLS on for a test table, then try a select with no policy and see zero rows.

title: localStorage only stores strings
why_it_matters: Saving an array directly gives you the useless text '[object Object]'.
explanation: localStorage keeps text only. Turn arrays and objects into a string with JSON.stringify before saving, and back with JSON.parse when reading. The ?? gives a safe default when nothing is saved yet.
try_it: Save an object, refresh the page, and read it back in the console.

title: Read a user's file without a server
why_it_matters: This is the base of every client-side file viewer or compressor.
explanation: The File API lets the browser read a file the user picks, entirely on their device. Nothing is uploaded. The file object has a name and methods like text() that return its contents.
try_it: Add an input of type file and log the size of any .txt file you pick.

title: Debounce search inputs
why_it_matters: It stops you firing a request on every single keystroke.
explanation: Debouncing waits until the user pauses before running your function. Each keystroke cancels the previous timer and starts a new one. Only the last timer survives to fire, so you send one request instead of many.
try_it: Log inside search() and compare the call count with and without the timer.

title: Commit small, commit often
why_it_matters: Small commits make bugs easy to find and easy to undo.
explanation: One commit should do one thing, with a message that says what. git add -p lets you pick which chunks of changes go in, so unrelated edits do not get bundled together.
code:
git add -p
git commit -m "Add login form validation"
git push
try_it: Make two unrelated edits, then commit them as two separate commits.

title: Never commit your .env file
why_it_matters: A leaked key on GitHub can be found and abused within minutes.
explanation: List secret files in .gitignore before the first commit. If a file is already tracked, git rm --cached stops tracking it. If a real key was already pushed, treat it as leaked and create a new one.
code:
echo ".env.local" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached .env.local
git commit -m "Stop tracking env file"
try_it: Open your repo's .gitignore and check your env files are listed.

title: Changed a Vercel variable? Redeploy
why_it_matters: It explains why the new value does not seem to work.
explanation: Environment variables are applied when a deployment is built or started. Editing one in the dashboard does not change deployments that already exist. Trigger a new deployment, and check the variable is set for the right environment.
try_it: Change a harmless variable, redeploy, and confirm the page shows the new value.

title: Spot hallucinated imports fast
why_it_matters: AI sometimes invents functions that sound completely real.
explanation: If an AI suggests a package or method you have never seen, do not assume it exists. Check your package.json, your editor's autocomplete, and the official docs. If none of them know it, it is probably made up.
try_it: Take the last AI answer you used and verify every import in it.

title: Make the AI explain line by line
why_it_matters: Understanding the code is the whole point of learning with AI.
explanation: Instead of only asking for a fix, paste the code and ask for each line explained. Tell it your level, for example: strong in HTML and CSS, new to JavaScript. Then explain it back in your own words.
try_it: Pick one function from your project and ask for a line-by-line explanation.

title: Paste the exact error, not a summary
why_it_matters: 'It does not work' gives the AI nothing to reason about.
explanation: Good debugging prompts include the full error text, the file it points to, and the code around that line. Add what you expected to happen and what happened instead. The more exact you are, the better the answer.
try_it: Next time something breaks, write the three parts down before you prompt.

title: Give every project a real README
why_it_matters: Recruiters often judge a repo by its README in seconds.
explanation: A short README should say what the project is, show how to run it, and list the tech used. Add one sentence on a problem you solved. It proves you can communicate, which is half of a developer's job.
try_it: Write a five-line README for your best project right now.

title: Build a tiny client-side file compressor
why_it_matters: A small, finished tool beats a big abandoned one.
explanation: Pick a project you can finish in a weekend. A browser tool that reads an image or text file, shrinks it, and offers a download needs no backend. It shows File API skills and is easy to demo.
try_it: Write down three features that fit one weekend, and cut one.

title: Pin your three best repos
why_it_matters: Your GitHub profile is often the first thing an employer opens.
explanation: GitHub lets you pin repositories at the top of your profile. Choose three that are finished, have a README, and show different skills. Add a short bio line saying what you are learning and looking for.
try_it: Pin three repos and read your profile as a stranger would.

title: Default to const, switch to let
why_it_matters: Fewer reassignments means fewer surprise bugs.
explanation: Use const for any value you never reassign, which is most of them. Use let only when the variable must change, like a counter. Reading code gets easier, because const promises that the name always points at the same thing.
try_it: Pick one let in your code, change it to const, and see if anything breaks.

title: Myth: var and let are the same
why_it_matters: Old tutorials still use var, and it leaks in ways that surprise you.
explanation: Fact: var ignores curly braces, so a variable made inside an if block or loop is still visible outside it. let and const stay inside their braces, which is what you'd expect. Modern code avoids var so variables can't leak into places you never planned.
try_it: Swap var for let on line 2 and predict what console.log(a) does now.

title: typeof null is a famous lie
why_it_matters: typeof is a handy check, but it has two traps.
explanation: typeof returns a value's type as text. It works for strings, numbers and booleans, but typeof null says 'object', an old mistake that can't be fixed. Arrays also say 'object'. Check null with === null, and arrays with Array.isArray.
code:
console.log(typeof "hi");       // string
console.log(typeof 42);         // number
console.log(typeof null);       // object
console.log(typeof []);         // object
console.log(Array.isArray([])); // true
try_it: Quiz: what is typeof undefined? And typeof a function? Check in the console.

title: Common mistake: ignoring the returned string
why_it_matters: Forgetting to save the result makes string methods look broken.
explanation: Strings can't be changed in place. Methods like trim and toUpperCase return a brand new string and leave the original alone. If you don't store or use the result, nothing seems to happen.
try_it: Quiz: does 'hello'.toUpperCase() change a variable that holds 'hello'?

title: Why '5' + 3 gives '53'
why_it_matters: This one explains half of all weird form-input bugs.
explanation: The + operator joins text if either side is a string. The other math operators, like - and *, convert strings into numbers instead. So the same inputs behave differently depending on the symbol. Convert with Number() before you add.
code:
console.log("5" + 3);         // 53
console.log("5" - 3);         // 2
console.log("5" * 3);         // 15
console.log(Number("5") + 3); // 8
try_it: Quiz: what does '10' / '2' give? Predict first, then test.

title: Number() or parseInt(): which one?
why_it_matters: Choosing wrong silently turns '12px' into 12 or NaN.
explanation: Number reads the whole string and gives NaN if anything is off. parseInt reads digits from the start and stops at the first non-digit, dropping any decimals. Use Number for strict checks and parseInt for things like '12px'. Pass 10 as the second argument to parseInt.
code:
console.log(Number("12px"));       // NaN
console.log(parseInt("12px", 10)); // 12
console.log(Number("3.5"));        // 3.5
console.log(parseInt("3.5", 10));  // 3
try_it: Run all four with the input '  42  ' and note which ones cope with spaces.

title: NaN is not equal to itself
why_it_matters: Checking for NaN the wrong way never works.
explanation: NaN means 'not a number', and it's the one value that isn't equal to itself, so === can't detect it. Use Number.isNaN(value). It returns true only for the real NaN, unlike the old global isNaN, which converts its input first.
code:
console.log(NaN === NaN);                 // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN));           // true
console.log(Number.isNaN("abc"));         // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(Number("abc"))); // true
try_it: Quiz: what is 'abc' * 2? Run it, then test the result with Number.isNaN.

title: null vs undefined in plain English
why_it_matters: Mixing them up makes data bugs harder to hunt down.
explanation: undefined means no value was ever set, like a missing property or an argument nobody passed. null means empty on purpose, a value you chose to set. Both are falsy, but they tell different stories when you're hunting a bug.
try_it: Declare a variable without a value and log it. Then set it to null on purpose.

title: The falsy values you must memorize
why_it_matters: Every if statement in JavaScript depends on this list.
explanation: JavaScript treats a few values as false inside an if: false, 0, an empty string, null, undefined and NaN. Everything else counts as true, including the string '0' and empty arrays or objects.
code:
const falsy = [false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN];
console.log(falsy.filter(Boolean).length); // 0
console.log(Boolean("0"));                 // true
console.log(Boolean([]));                  // true
try_it: Quiz: is the string 'false' truthy or falsy? Test it with Boolean('false').

title: Myth: == is just a looser ===
why_it_matters: Loose equality hides type conversions that break real logic.
explanation: Fact: == converts types before comparing, using rules that are hard to predict. === compares type and value with no conversion, so it does what it looks like it does. Default to === everywhere and you'll rarely get surprised.
code:
console.log(0 == "");   // true
console.log("1" == 1);  // true
console.log(0 === "");  // false
console.log("1" === 1); // false
try_it: Search your code for a double-equals comparison and change it to ===.

title: Common mistake: || turns 0 into a default
why_it_matters: A quantity or discount of 0 is valid data, not 'missing'.
explanation: || falls back for any falsy value, including 0, false and an empty string. ?? falls back only for null or undefined. If zero or an empty string is a legitimate value, like a quantity, use ?? so you don't overwrite it by accident.
code:
const qty = 0;
console.log(qty || 10);  // 10 (wrong, 0 was valid)
console.log(qty ?? 10);  // 0  (right)
console.log(null ?? 10); // 10
try_it: Find one || default in your code and ask: could 0 or '' be valid there?

title: Ternary: a one-line if/else
why_it_matters: You'll see this in almost every React component.
explanation: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse is an expression, so it produces a value you can store or drop straight into JSX. Keep it for one simple choice. Once you need to nest ternaries, switch to a normal if/else.
try_it: Turn one small if/else in your code into a ternary.

title: && works as a tiny if
why_it_matters: It's the trick behind 'show this only when that is true'.
explanation: a && b gives back a if it's falsy, otherwise b. That makes it a shortcut for 'if a, then b'. Be careful when the left side can be 0: you'll get 0 back, and in React that 0 shows on screen.
code:
const isLoggedIn = true;
console.log(isLoggedIn && "Welcome back"); // Welcome back
console.log(false && "never seen");        // false
console.log(0 && "never seen");            // 0
try_it: Predict the output of '' && 'hi' before you run it.

title: Set a default once with ??=
why_it_matters: It replaces a clunky if (x === undefined) block.
explanation: a ??= b means: assign b only if a is null or undefined. It's the short way to fill in a default. There's also ||= and &&=, but ??= is the safest because it keeps real values like 0 and an empty string.
try_it: Add a missing default to an object in your code using ??=.

title: Before vs after: switch vs lookup
why_it_matters: A lookup object is shorter and easier to extend.
explanation: When a switch only turns one value into another, an object does the same job with less code. Look up the key, and use ?? for the fallback. It's easier to read, test and extend when you add a new status.
try_it: Find a switch in your code that only returns values and swap it for an object.

title: Quiz: round, floor, ceil, trunc
why_it_matters: Rounding prices and page counts needs the right one.
explanation: round goes to the nearest whole number. floor always goes down, ceil always goes up, and trunc just chops off the decimals. floor and trunc agree for positive numbers but differ for negatives: floor(-2.9) is -3, trunc(-2.9) is -2.
code:
console.log(Math.round(2.5));  // 3
console.log(Math.floor(2.9));  // 2
console.log(Math.ceil(2.1));   // 3
console.log(Math.floor(-2.9)); // -3
console.log(Math.trunc(-2.9)); // -2
try_it: Quiz: how many pages do you need for 25 items at 10 per page? Use Math.ceil.

title: Before vs after: guard clauses
why_it_matters: Flat code is easier to read, especially on a small screen.
explanation: Instead of wrapping everything in nested if blocks, handle the bad cases first and return straight away. The main logic then sits at the bottom with no extra indentation. Each early return removes one level of nesting.
try_it: Find a function with three nested ifs and flip it into early returns.

title: Anatomy of a for loop
why_it_matters: Every other loop idea builds on these three parts.
explanation: A for loop has three parts: where to start, when to keep going, and what changes each round. JavaScript counts from 0, and i < 3 stops before 3, so this loop runs three times, not four.
try_it: Change the loop to count from 1 to 5 instead.

title: for...of: loop over the values
why_it_matters: It's the cleanest way to visit every item in an array.
explanation: for...of hands you each item directly, with no index to manage. It reads almost like English: for each tool of tools. Choose it when you just need the values, or when you want to use break, continue or await inside the loop.
try_it: Rewrite a for loop in your code that only uses i to read tools[i].

title: Common mistake: for...in on arrays
why_it_matters: It returns index strings, not the items you wanted.
explanation: for...in loops over an object's keys. On an array, those keys are index strings like '0', not the items, so you'll get the wrong thing. Use for...of for arrays, and keep for...in for plain objects when you need keys.
try_it: Run both loops and compare what the loop variable holds each time.

title: Infinite loops freeze your tab
why_it_matters: One forgotten line can lock up the browser.
explanation: A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true. If nothing inside ever makes it false, the loop never stops and your tab freezes. Before running any loop, ask yourself: what eventually makes this condition false?
try_it: Quiz: how many times does this print if tries starts at 5?

title: break vs continue, side by side
why_it_matters: Two small keywords that control loops precisely.
explanation: continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. break leaves the loop completely. Both work in for, for...of and while loops. Neither works inside forEach, because the loop body there is a separate function.
try_it: Quiz: change break to continue. What prints now?

title: forEach does not wait for await
why_it_matters: This bug makes code run in an order you didn't expect.
explanation: forEach ignores whatever your callback returns, so it won't wait for async functions, and you can't break out of it. Here, 'finished?' prints before any 'done'. When you need await or an early exit, use a for...of loop.
try_it: Rewrite this with for...of inside an async function and compare the order.

title: Loop over an object with entries
why_it_matters: Plain objects can't be used with for...of directly.
explanation: Object.entries turns an object into an array of [key, value] pairs. Combine it with for...of and destructuring to read both at once. It's the cleanest way to loop over an object, and it works with break and continue too.
try_it: Add a third item to the object and see the loop pick it up.

title: Three ways to write a function
why_it_matters: You'll meet all three in real code, so learn to read each.
explanation: A declaration starts with the function keyword. An expression stores a function in a variable. An arrow function is a shorter expression. All three create something you can call. Arrow functions are the most common in modern React and Next.js code.
try_it: Rewrite add as an arrow function without looking at the others.

title: Common mistake: arrow braces need return
why_it_matters: You get undefined and no error to point at the bug.
explanation: Without braces, an arrow function returns its expression automatically. With braces, it's a normal function body, so you must write return yourself. Forgetting it is a classic bug that silently hands back undefined.
code:
const double = (n) => n * 2;           // implicit return
const triple = (n) => { return n * 3; };
const broken = (n) => { n * 4 };       // no return!
console.log(double(2), triple(2), broken(2)); // 4 6 undefined
try_it: Fix broken so it returns 8 when called with 2.

title: Returning an object from an arrow
why_it_matters: Without parentheses, JavaScript thinks the braces are a function body.
explanation: Curly braces after an arrow are read as a function body, not an object. Wrap the object in parentheses so JavaScript sees a value. You'll need this all the time with map, like users.map(u => ({ id: u.id })).
try_it: Use map with an arrow to turn [1, 2, 3] into [{ n: 1 }, { n: 2 }, { n: 3 }].

title: No return means undefined
why_it_matters: Printing a value and returning it are not the same thing.
explanation: A function only gives something back when you use return. Without it you get undefined, even if the function printed something on screen. Printing shows a value to you, while returning hands it to the code that called the function.
try_it: Change show so it returns the message in upper case instead of printing it.

title: Default parameters in one line
why_it_matters: They make your functions safe when an argument is missing.
explanation: Give a parameter a default value with =. It's used only when the argument is missing or undefined. This replaces the old pattern name = name || 'friend', which also overwrote valid falsy values like 0.
try_it: Add a second parameter, punctuation, that defaults to an exclamation mark.

title: Rest parameters collect the extras
why_it_matters: One function can accept any number of inputs.
explanation: ...nums gathers all the remaining arguments into a real array, so one function can take any number of inputs. The rest parameter must come last. Don't confuse it with spread, which does the opposite and unpacks an array.
try_it: Write maxOf(...nums) using Math.max and spread.

title: Parameters vs arguments, finally clear
why_it_matters: Argument order mistakes give wrong answers with no error.
explanation: Parameters are the names in a function's definition. Arguments are the real values you pass when calling it. JavaScript matches them by position, not by name, so swapping two arguments silently gives a wrong result.
try_it: Change discount to take one object, { price, percent }, so order can't matter.

title: Pure functions are easy to trust
why_it_matters: React expects your components to behave this way.
explanation: A pure function uses only its inputs and changes nothing outside itself. The same input always gives the same output. That makes it simple to test and debug. Impure functions depend on, or change, things elsewhere, so results can vary.
try_it: List one pure and one impure function from your own project.

title: Callbacks: pass a function in
why_it_matters: Click handlers, timers and map all work this way.
explanation: Functions are values, so you can pass one into another. The receiving function calls it when ready, and that's a callback. Event listeners, timers and array methods like map all use callbacks. Pass the function itself, not its result.
try_it: Call repeat with a callback that logs only even rounds.

title: Common mistake: calling instead of passing
why_it_matters: Adding () runs the function right now, not later.
explanation: sayHi() with parentheses runs the function immediately and passes its result along. sayHi without them hands over the function itself, to be called later. This slip breaks setTimeout, event listeners, and React onClick handlers.
try_it: In your browser console, try the wrong line and watch when 'Hi' appears.

title: Why you can call functions early
why_it_matters: Hoisting explains confusing 'before initialization' errors.
explanation: JavaScript reads function declarations before running anything, so you can call them above where they're written. let, const, and arrow functions stored in const don't work that way. Touching them early throws a ReferenceError. Define things before you use them and you're safe.
try_it: Move the add declaration to the bottom of your file and check it still works.

title: Inner functions see outer variables
why_it_matters: This is the idea behind scope, and later behind closures.
explanation: A function can read variables from the places around where it was written, but outer code can't see inside it. JavaScript looks in the current scope first, then moves outward. That lookup path is called the scope chain.
try_it: Uncomment the last line and read the error message carefully.

title: Closures remember their variables
why_it_matters: Event handlers and React hooks rely on this every day.
explanation: When a function is created, it keeps access to the variables around it, even after the outer function has finished. That memory is a closure. Here, count lives on privately between calls, and nothing outside can touch it.
try_it: Create a second counter and check that it starts again at 1.

title: Quiz: why does var print 3, 3, 3?
why_it_matters: A classic interview question, and a real source of bugs.
explanation: var shares one variable across the whole loop, so every callback sees its final value, 3, by the time the timers fire. let creates a fresh variable for each round, so each callback remembers its own number.
try_it: Predict all six lines of output before running it.

title: Recursion in plain English
why_it_matters: Nested data like folders and comment threads needs it.
explanation: Recursion means a function calling itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a stopping case, called the base case, or it never ends. Here n === 0 stops the chain. Great for nested data such as folders or replies.
try_it: Write sumTo(n) that adds 1 + 2 + ... + n using recursion.

title: this depends on how you call it
why_it_matters: A lost 'this' is behind many broken event handlers.
explanation: Inside a method, this means whatever sits before the dot when you call it. Pull the method out into a variable and that link is lost. bind(user) locks this to a chosen object. Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the surrounding one.
try_it: Remove .bind(user), call hi() as a plain function, and read the result.

title: Functions can return functions
why_it_matters: This pattern powers helpers, middleware and many React tools.
explanation: Because functions are values, one function can build and return another. multiplyBy remembers factor through a closure, so each function it creates has its own multiplier. It's a handy way to create small custom helpers from one template.
try_it: Build addTax(rate) that returns a function adding that tax to a price.

title: push, pop, shift, unshift cheat sheet
why_it_matters: Four methods cover most array edits you'll ever make.
explanation: push and pop work on the end of an array. unshift and shift work on the start. All four change the original array. pop and shift also return the item they removed, which makes them handy for stacks and queues.
code:
const q = ["b", "c"];
q.push("d");            // end:   b c d
q.unshift("a");         // start: a b c d
console.log(q.pop());   // d
console.log(q.shift()); // a
console.log(q);         // ["b", "c"]
try_it: Quiz: for [1, 2], what is left after q.push(9), q.pop(), q.shift()?

title: Get the last item with at(-1)
why_it_matters: It's shorter, and harder to get wrong than length - 1.
explanation: Square brackets can't take negative indexes, so the old way to get the last item was length - 1. The at method accepts negative numbers and counts from the end. at(-1) is the last item, at(-2) the one before it.
code:
const scores = [70, 85, 92];
console.log(scores[scores.length - 1]); // 92
console.log(scores.at(-1));             // 92
console.log(scores.at(-2));             // 85
try_it: Use at(-1) to get the last character of 'DevTok'. Strings have at too.

title: filter keeps only what matches
why_it_matters: It's how you build search results and category tabs.
explanation: filter runs a test on each item and keeps the ones where your function returns true. You get a new array, which may be shorter or even empty. Unlike map, the number of items can change, but the items themselves stay the same.
try_it: Filter the array to keep only prices between 100 and 200.

title: find returns one, filter returns many
why_it_matters: Mixing them up gives you an array when you wanted an object.
explanation: find returns the first matching item itself, or undefined if nothing matches. filter returns an array of every match. Looking up one record by id? Use find. Building a shorter list? Use filter.
try_it: Quiz: what does filter return when nothing matches, an empty array or undefined?

title: some and every answer yes or no
why_it_matters: They replace messy loops with a single readable line.
explanation: some asks: does at least one item pass the test? every asks: do all items pass? Both return true or false and stop as soon as they know. One quirk: every on an empty array is true, because nothing fails.
code:
const ages = [17, 22, 30];
console.log(ages.some((a) => a < 18));   // true
console.log(ages.every((a) => a >= 18)); // false
console.log([].every((a) => a > 100));   // true
try_it: Use every to check that all strings in ['a', 'b', ''] are non-empty.

title: Common mistake: indexOf in an if
why_it_matters: -1 is truthy, so a missing item can pass the check.
explanation: To check whether an array holds something, includes gives a clear true or false. indexOf returns a position, and -1 when the item is missing. Since -1 is truthy, if (list.indexOf(x)) is wrong in both directions: missing passes, and position 0 fails.
try_it: Replace one indexOf check in your code with includes.

title: reduce turns a list into one value
why_it_matters: Totals, counts and lookups all come from the same idea.
explanation: reduce walks through the array carrying an accumulator. Each round your function gets the running result and the current item, and returns the new result. The second argument, 0, is the starting value. Perfect for sums, counts and building objects.
try_it: Use reduce to find the largest number in [3, 9, 4].

title: Common mistake: reduce without a start
why_it_matters: It crashes on empty lists and breaks on arrays of objects.
explanation: If you skip the second argument, reduce uses the first item as the starting total. That breaks with arrays of objects, and it throws an error on an empty array. Always pass a start value: 0 for sums, [] for lists, {} for objects.
code:
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)); // 0 (safe)
const objs = [{ n: 1 }, { n: 2 }];
console.log(objs.reduce((a, b) => a + b.n));    // [object Object]2
console.log(objs.reduce((a, b) => a + b.n, 0)); // 3
try_it: Remove the 0 from the first line and read the error you get.

title: sort() compares as text by default
why_it_matters: Numbers sort in an order that looks completely wrong.
explanation: Without a compare function, sort converts items to strings and compares them letter by letter, so '10' comes before '9'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for ascending numbers, or b - a for descending.
code:
const nums = [10, 9, 1, 100];
console.log([...nums].sort());                // [1, 10, 100, 9]
console.log([...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b)); // [1, 9, 10, 100]
console.log([...nums].sort((a, b) => b - a)); // [100, 10, 9, 1]
try_it: Quiz: where does 100 land in the default sort of [5, 100, 25]? Check it.

title: sort changes the original array
why_it_matters: It can silently break other code, and React state.
explanation: sort rearranges the array in place, which quietly changes data other code may be using. Copy first with [...arr], then sort the copy. Newer browsers also have toSorted, which returns a sorted copy and leaves the original alone.
try_it: Log an array before and after calling sort directly on it.

title: slice copies, splice edits
why_it_matters: One letter apart, but one is safe and one is not.
explanation: slice(start, end) returns a piece of the array and leaves the original alone; the end index isn't included. splice changes the original by removing or inserting items. Memory trick: splice is surgery on the array itself.
code:
const letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"];
console.log(letters.slice(1, 3)); // ["b", "c"]
console.log(letters);             // unchanged
letters.splice(1, 2);             // removes "b" and "c"
console.log(letters);             // ["a", "d"]
try_it: Use slice to get the first two items of any array of five.

title: Myth: b = a makes a copy
why_it_matters: Shared arrays cause bugs where changing one list alters another.
explanation: Fact: assigning an array to another variable doesn't copy it, both names point to the same array. Spread, [...a], builds a new array with the same items. It's the basic move for changing data without damaging the original.
try_it: Quiz: what does c hold if you push 4 into a after copying? Run it.

title: Merge arrays with spread
why_it_matters: Add or combine items in any position, in one line.
explanation: Spread unpacks an array's items into a new one, so you can merge arrays and insert items anywhere in a single line. It reads like the result you want, and it never changes the originals.
try_it: Build a new array with 'Git' added at the start of all.

title: Array.from builds arrays from anything
why_it_matters: Handy for page numbers, placeholder items and Sets.
explanation: Array.from creates an array from anything list-like or iterable, such as a string or a Set. Give it an object with just a length, plus a mapping function, and you can generate sequences like page numbers or dummy items for testing.
code:
console.log(Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i + 1)); // [1, 2, 3]
console.log(Array.from("abc"));                          // ["a", "b", "c"]
console.log(Array.from(new Set([1, 1, 2])));             // [1, 2]
try_it: Generate [10, 20, 30, 40] with Array.from and a mapping function.

title: flat and flatMap untangle nesting
why_it_matters: Nested arrays show up in API data all the time.
explanation: flat removes one level of nesting from an array. flatMap maps each item and then flattens the result by one level, in a single step. It's useful when each item turns into several items, like splitting sentences into words.
try_it: Flatten [[1], [2, [3]]] with flat(), then try flat(2).

title: split and join: strings and arrays
why_it_matters: They are opposites, and together they solve many small tasks.
explanation: split cuts a string into an array at a separator. join glues an array back into a string with the separator you choose. Together they handle CSV text, URL parts and class names without any loops.
try_it: Turn 'my cool title' into 'my-cool-title' using split and join.

title: Array destructuring unpacks by position
why_it_matters: This is exactly how you read useState in React.
explanation: Destructuring pulls items out of an array into named variables, by position. ...rest collects the leftovers. As a bonus, [x, y] = [y, x] swaps two variables without a temporary one. React's useState returns an array, so you destructure it.
try_it: Swap two variables of your own using destructuring.

title: Chain filter and map together
why_it_matters: Real UI lists usually need both: pick items, then shape them.
explanation: Array methods return arrays, so you can chain them. Filter first to pick the items, then map to reshape them. Read left to right it tells a story: keep in-stock products, then take their names. Filtering first also means less work for map.
try_it: Extend the chain so it also requires a price over 600.

title: Remove an item without mutating
why_it_matters: This is the standard way to delete from React state.
explanation: To delete an item from a list, use filter to keep everything except that one. You get a new array while the old one stays intact. React notices the new array and updates the screen, which wouldn't happen if you edited the original.
try_it: Write removeById(list, id) that returns a new array and never edits the old one.

title: Update one item with map
why_it_matters: Toggling a todo or editing a row needs exactly this move.
explanation: Map over the array and return a changed copy of the matching item, while keeping all the others as they are. Spread copies the old fields, then you override one. The original array and object stay untouched, which is what React state needs.
try_it: Change the code so it toggles done, true to false and back, instead of setting it.

title: Remove duplicates with a Set
why_it_matters: A Set is the shortest path from messy to unique.
explanation: A Set stores each value only once. Pass an array in and duplicates vanish. Spread the Set back into an array and you're done. It works for numbers and strings; objects are compared by reference, so look-alike objects stay.
try_it: Use a Set to count how many different letters are in 'banana'.

title: Empty arrays are truthy
why_it_matters: An empty list can pass an if check and show a blank screen.
explanation: An empty array counts as true in an if, so if (results) passes even with zero items. To check whether a list has anything in it, use results.length. Zero is falsy and anything higher is truthy.
try_it: Add an empty-state message check to one list in your project.

title: Dot vs bracket notation
why_it_matters: Picking the wrong one is a classic 'why is it undefined' bug.
explanation: Dot notation is the short way when you know the key name. Use brackets when the key is stored in a variable, or contains characters like a hyphen or a space. user.field looks for a key literally named field, which is a common mistake.
try_it: Quiz: why is the last line undefined? Fix it so it prints Ada.

title: Shorthand property names
why_it_matters: You'll see this in nearly every modern code example.
explanation: When a variable has the same name as the key you want, write it once. { name, age } means the same as { name: name, age: age }. It's especially handy when building objects to send to an API.
try_it: Create an object from three variables using only shorthand.

title: Computed keys: build a key on the fly
why_it_matters: One change handler can then update any form field.
explanation: Square brackets inside an object literal evaluate the expression and use the result as the key. This is how a single onChange handler can update any form field: it builds { [e.target.name]: e.target.value } for whichever input fired.
try_it: Write setField(obj, key, value) that returns a copy with that key changed.

title: Destructure objects by key name
why_it_matters: It's how React components read their props.
explanation: Object destructuring pulls out properties by name, not by position. Take only the ones you need. It's the standard way to read props in React components and fields from API responses.
try_it: Destructure two fields from any object in your project.

title: Destructuring: rename and set defaults
why_it_matters: It turns messy incoming data into clean, predictable variables.
explanation: Write key: newName to rename a property while destructuring. Write = value to give it a default when the key is missing or undefined. Defaults ignore null, so null stays null. Use both together to tidy messy API data.
try_it: Quiz: what would plan be if it was null instead of undefined?

title: Spread copies and updates objects
why_it_matters: It's how you 'change' an object without mutating it.
explanation: { ...user } copies every property into a new object. Properties written after the spread override the copied ones, so put your changes last. The original object stays exactly as it was, which is what React state updates need.
try_it: Move plan: 'pro' before ...user and see why the override stops working.

title: Spread only copies one level deep
why_it_matters: Nested data stays shared, and edits leak into the original.
explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects and arrays are still shared between the copy and the original, so changing one changes both. structuredClone makes a deep copy where nested data is fully independent. It can't copy functions, though.
try_it: Quiz: after the code runs, what does c.skills contain?

title: Object.keys and Object.values
why_it_matters: Plain objects have no length or map, but these fix that.
explanation: Plain objects don't have map or length, but these helpers turn them into arrays that do. keys gives the names, values gives the data. Object.keys(obj).length is the usual way to count properties.
code:
const stock = { tea: 5, rice: 0 };
console.log(Object.keys(stock));        // ["tea", "rice"]
console.log(Object.values(stock));      // [5, 0]
console.log(Object.keys(stock).length); // 2
try_it: Use Object.values and reduce to total up the stock numbers.

title: Object.fromEntries rebuilds an object
why_it_matters: It's map for objects, and it's easier than it looks.
explanation: Object.entries turns an object into pairs, you map those pairs, and fromEntries turns them back into an object. Use it to transform every value in an object, like applying a discount to all prices.
try_it: Change the callback so it adds 100 to every price instead.

title: Key exists vs value is truthy
why_it_matters: A value of 0 exists, but a truthy check says it doesn't.
explanation: To ask whether a key exists, use Object.hasOwn or the in operator. Testing the value itself, like if (stock.tea), fails when the value is falsy: tea exists with 0, but the check says it's missing. Existence and truthiness are different questions.
code:
const stock = { tea: 0 };
console.log(Object.hasOwn(stock, "tea"));        // true
console.log("tea" in stock);                     // true
console.log(stock.tea ? "in stock" : "missing"); // missing (wrong!)
console.log(Object.hasOwn(stock, "milk"));       // false
try_it: Check a key in one of your own objects using Object.hasOwn.

title: Myth: two equal objects are ===
why_it_matters: This is why React sometimes re-renders when nothing changed.
explanation: Fact: === on objects and arrays checks whether both names point at the very same object, not whether their contents match. Two separate objects with identical contents aren't equal. A new object each render means a new reference.
try_it: Quiz: is [] === [] true or false? Then check it.

title: Map: a smarter lookup table
why_it_matters: Use it when keys change a lot or aren't plain strings.
explanation: A Map stores key-value pairs like an object, but keys can be anything, it remembers insertion order, and it has a size. Use a Map for lookup tables that change often. Use plain objects for fixed-shape records.
try_it: Store two keys in a Map and read one back.

title: JSON.stringify and JSON.parse
why_it_matters: Saving data and sending it to an API both rely on this pair.
explanation: JSON is text. stringify turns a JavaScript value into JSON text so you can save or send it, and parse turns the text back into a value. stringify drops functions and undefined, so JSON is for plain data only.
try_it: Stringify an object, log the text, then parse it back.

title: JSON.parse throws on bad text
why_it_matters: One bad string from storage can crash your whole page.
explanation: JSON.parse throws an error if the text isn't valid JSON, like text someone edited by hand or a failed response. Wrap it in try/catch and return a fallback so your app doesn't crash. JSON needs double quotes around keys and strings.
try_it: Call safeParse with an empty string and see what comes back.

title: Decode: Cannot read properties of undefined
why_it_matters: It's the most common JavaScript error you will ever see.
explanation: This error means the thing before the dot is undefined or null. The message names the property you tried to read. Work backwards: where was this variable supposed to get its value? Usually the data hasn't loaded yet, or the name is wrong.
try_it: Trigger this error on purpose, then fix it with optional chaining.

title: Throw your own errors
why_it_matters: Failing loudly beats returning a wrong number quietly.
explanation: throw stops a function and sends an error up to the nearest catch. Throw an Error object, not a plain string, so you get a message and a stack trace. Validate inputs at the start so bad data can't produce wrong results.
try_it: Add a second check that throws when amount is negative.

title: finally always runs
why_it_matters: It's the right place for cleanup like hiding a spinner.
explanation: The finally block runs whether the try worked or threw an error. Use it for cleanup, like hiding a loading spinner or re-enabling a button, so you don't repeat that code in both the success and failure branches.
try_it: Remove the throw line and check that finally still runs.

title: console.table beats console.log for lists
why_it_matters: Small debugging habits save a lot of squinting.
explanation: console.table prints an array of objects as a neat table. Wrapping a variable in braces, console.log({ users }), also prints its name as a label, so you always know which value is which. Small habits that make debugging faster.
try_it: Use console.table on an array from your own project.

title: Pause your code with debugger
why_it_matters: Stepping through code beats scattering ten console.logs.
explanation: The debugger keyword pauses your code at that line when DevTools is open. You can then inspect every variable and step forward one line at a time. Remove it before you commit.
try_it: Add debugger to a loop, open DevTools, and press F10 to step.

title: Quiz: why does timeout 0 print last?
why_it_matters: Understanding this order removes a lot of async confusion.
explanation: setTimeout schedules a function for later, and even with 0 milliseconds it waits until the current code has finished. JavaScript does one thing at a time, so timers wait in a queue for their turn.
try_it: Add a fourth console.log after the timeout and predict where it appears.

title: A Promise is an IOU for a value
why_it_matters: fetch and nearly every modern async API returns one.
explanation: A Promise is an object standing in for a value that isn't ready yet. It starts pending, then either fulfills with a result or rejects with an error. Use then to run code when it fulfills, and catch to handle a rejection.
try_it: Chain a second then that logs 'and again' after the first one.

title: Before vs after: then vs await
why_it_matters: await makes async code read like normal top-to-bottom code.
explanation: await pauses an async function until a promise is ready, then hands you the result, so the code reads top to bottom. It works inside functions marked async. Behind the scenes it's still promises, so everything you learn about them still applies.
try_it: Take one .then chain in your code and rewrite it with await.

title: async functions always return a Promise
why_it_matters: It explains why you sometimes log a Promise instead of data.
explanation: Even if you return a plain value, an async function wraps it in a promise. To read the value, use await inside another async function, or use .then. A frequent bug is printing the function's result and wondering why you see a Promise.
try_it: Call it with await inside another async function and log the number.

title: Catch async errors with try/catch
why_it_matters: Without it, a failed request leaves the user staring at nothing.
explanation: When an awaited promise rejects, await throws the error at that line, so ordinary try/catch can catch it. Without a catch you get an unhandled rejection and the user sees nothing happen. Always decide what the user should see when a request fails.
try_it: Add a finally block that logs 'done' whether or not it failed.

title: fetch does not throw on a 404
why_it_matters: Most beginner fetch code misses this and shows broken pages.
explanation: fetch only rejects when the network itself fails. A 404 or 500 response still counts as a success, so res.json() may fail or give you an error page. Check res.ok and throw your own error when it's false.
try_it: Call getJson on a URL that doesn't exist and read the error you throw.

title: POST JSON with fetch
why_it_matters: Every form, login and booking in your apps does this.
explanation: For a POST you pass an options object: the method, a Content-Type header saying the body is JSON, and the body as a JSON string. Forgetting JSON.stringify sends the useless text '[object Object]'.
try_it: Write the same call for another endpoint, like /api/bookings, with two fields.

title: Promise.all runs tasks together
why_it_matters: Independent requests should not wait in line.
explanation: Promise.all starts several promises at once and waits until all finish, giving you an array of results in the same order. If any one fails, the whole thing rejects. Use it for independent requests, like loading a profile and its orders.
try_it: Time it with console.time to prove it takes about 300ms, not 600.

title: await in a loop runs one by one
why_it_matters: Sometimes that is right, and sometimes it is slow.
explanation: An await inside a for loop pauses each round, so tasks run one after another. That's correct when order matters or the next step needs the last result. For independent requests, start them together with Promise.all and your total wait shrinks a lot.
try_it: Rewrite slow() with Promise.all and map so it takes about 200ms.

title: Promise.allSettled keeps going after failures
why_it_matters: Use it when partial success is still a success.
explanation: Promise.all gives up if one promise fails. Promise.allSettled waits for every one and reports what happened to each, with a status and a value or reason. Use it when partial success is fine, like loading several dashboard widgets.
try_it: Log the reason of the rejected result as well.

title: Loading, error, success: model all three
why_it_matters: Every screen with data needs these three states.
explanation: Every request has three moments: waiting, success and failure. Model them with a status value, and your UI always has something honest to show: a spinner, the data, or a retry message. Skipping this makes screens flash empty or freeze.
try_it: Sketch what your UI shows in each of the three states.

title: Cancel stale fetches with AbortController
why_it_matters: Fast typing can make old results overwrite new ones.
explanation: If a user types fast, old requests can finish after newer ones and show stale results. An AbortController lets you cancel the earlier fetch: pass its signal, call abort(), and the promise rejects with an AbortError you can safely ignore.
try_it: Create a new controller for each search and abort the previous one.

title: Quiz: promises beat timers, even at 0
why_it_matters: It explains odd orderings in your console logs.
explanation: JavaScript runs normal code first, then promise callbacks, then timers. Promise callbacks sit in a faster queue called the microtask queue. So even a 0ms timeout loses to an already-resolved promise.
try_it: Predict the order if you add a second Promise.resolve().then(...) line.

title: setInterval needs a clearInterval
why_it_matters: Forgotten intervals keep running and leak memory.
explanation: setInterval repeats a function every set number of milliseconds and returns an id. Pass that id to clearInterval to stop it. Forgetting to stop intervals keeps them running forever, which in React means leaks when a component unmounts.
try_it: Change it to stop after five ticks, then run it.

title: Myth: await freezes the whole page
why_it_matters: Knowing this keeps you from fearing await in click handlers.
explanation: Fact: await pauses only the async function it's inside. The rest of your page, including clicks and animations, keeps running, because the browser is free to do other work while it waits. Code after the call runs straight away.
try_it: Quiz: which line prints first if you add await before slow()?

title: Common mistake: months start at 0
why_it_matters: Showing the wrong month on a booking screen looks careless.
explanation: In JavaScript dates, months are numbered 0 to 11, so January is 0 and December is 11, while days start at 1. Add 1 when you show a month number to users. For display, toLocaleDateString saves you the maths.
code:
const d = new Date(2026, 0, 15); // month 0 = January
console.log(d.getMonth());       // 0
console.log(d.getMonth() + 1);   // 1
console.log(d.getFullYear());    // 2026
console.log(d.toLocaleDateString("en-GB")); // 15/01/2026
try_it: Create a date for 25 December and print its month number.
